definition.text: A wetland that builds up peat, a deposit of dead plant matter, usually sphagnum moss.

facts.text: Bogs are one of the four main types of wetland; alkaline peat-forming mires are called fens instead.
They form where surface water is acidic and poor in nutrients, mostly in cooler northern climates.
Plants grow slowly, but decay is even slower in the oxygen-poor waterlogged soil, so peat piles up, sometimes many meters deep.
Most bogs get their water and nutrients from rain rather than ground or surface water, and have peat usually thicker than 30 centimetres.
The world's largest wetland is the peat bogs of the Western Siberian Lowlands, covering more than a million square kilometres.
Bogs host specialized species, such as carnivorous sundews and pitcher plants that get nutrients from insects.
Slowly accumulating plant material makes bogs a carbon sink.

definition.text: The classes of bog defined by landscape position, water source and nutrient supply, such as valley, raised, blanket and quaking bogs.

facts.text: Valley bogs form in gently sloping hollows and, because they rely on ground or surface water, occur only on acidic ground.
Raised bogs grow over centuries from a lake through marsh and fen until a rain-fed peat dome a few meters high forms.
Blanket bogs cover hilltops and slopes in cool places with rain on more than c. 235 days a year.
Quaking bogs are floating mats of moss and sedge, about half a meter thick, that move when walked on.

definition.text: Cutting peat from bogs to burn as fuel or to sell as a garden soil improver.

facts.text: Peat supplies more than 20% of home heat in Ireland and is burned for fuel in Finland, Scotland, Germany and Russia.
Russia is the leading exporter of fuel peat, at more than 90 million metric tons per year.
Because peat builds up so slowly, a bog is hard to restore once the peat is gone.
More than 90% of England's bogs have been damaged or destroyed, and in 2011 the UK announced plans to remove peat from gardening products.

definition.text: The benefits intact bogs give people, chiefly carbon storage and fresh water, along with food and recreation.

facts.text: If bog peat decays, its carbon escapes as carbon dioxide and adds to global warming; left undisturbed, bogs remain a carbon sink.
The peatlands of the former Soviet Union were calculated to remove 52 Tg of carbon per year from the atmosphere.
Rewetting drained peatlands may be among the most cost-effective ways to mitigate climate change.
Peat bogs store fresh water near the headwaters of large rivers; the Yangtze rises in the Ruoergai peatland.
Wild blueberries, cranberries, cloudberries and lingonberries are harvested from bogs, which are also used for ecotourism and hunting.

definition.text: The drying, drainage and warming that are degrading bogs, which take thousands of years to form and are very hard to recover.

facts.text: Northern European sphagnum bogs were often cleared and drained for farming, and European peatlands have dried quickly in recent centuries from drainage, peat cutting and burning.
Many Arctic and sub-Arctic bogs are warming at 0.6 °C per decade, twice the global average, and releasing large amounts of greenhouse gases.
These changes have caused severe declines in peatland biodiversity across Northern Europe.
Bogs are recognized as priority habitats by many agencies, including the UK Biodiversity Action Plan.

definition.text: A subarctic ecosystem of the Northern Hemisphere, roughly between 50° and 70°N, commonly called taiga.

facts.text: Boreal ecosystems span parts of North America, Europe and Asia.
Their plants range from black and white spruce to willows, wildflowers and alders, and caribou move in during winter to eat lichen.
They are less diverse than tropical systems but still hold a variety of species.
Wildfires, floods, mudslides and insect outbreaks drive secondary succession, which keeps the forest cycling.
Boreal soils hold about 338 Pg of carbon, comparable to the carbon in tropical ecosystems' biomass.
They are among the ecosystems most vulnerable to climate change.

definition.text: How warming changes boreal ecosystems and how their changes feed back on the climate.

facts.text: Thawing permafrost, milder winters and hotter summers displace cold-adapted species, increase forest fires and can turn boreal areas into other ecosystem types.
Plants and animals are already shifting northward, though plant migration may lag warming by decades to a century.
Permafrost thaw, fire and insect outbreaks have led some models to suggest boreal forests are now a net carbon source rather than a sink.
Permafrost stores double the carbon now in the atmosphere, which thawing can release as greenhouse gases.

definition.text: The services boreal ecosystems provide, led by timber and climate regulation through carbon cycling.

facts.text: Canada's boreal ecosystem is one of the world's largest carbon reservoirs and has high hydroelectric potential.
Boreal forests supply lumber and regulate water, soil and air quality.
Managing an ecosystem to maximize one service tends to reduce the supply of the others.

definition.text: The part of the ocean below about 200 m (660 ft), where light fades and the continental shelf gives way to the slope.

facts.text: It is cold, dark and under high pressure, and is the least explored biome on Earth.
Pressure rises about 1 atmosphere every 10 meters, reaching more than 1,000 atmospheres in places.
Without light there is no photosynthesis, so life depends on food sinking from above or on chemical energy at vents.
Its temperature is almost unchanging over long periods; no other habitat on Earth is so constant.
Salinity stays at about 35 parts per thousand throughout.
In 1960 the bathyscaphe Trieste reached the bottom of the Mariana Trench at 10,911 m, the deepest known spot in any ocean.
Deep-sea fish tend to be small, with slow metabolisms, and many use bioluminescence to hide their silhouettes.

definition.text: Organic material such as algae fragments, detritus and waste that drifts down from sunlit surface waters into the deep sea.

facts.text: Many deep-sea organisms survive by feeding on marine snow.
Sinking organic matter falls at approximately 100 meters per day, and only about 1 to 3% of surface production reaches the seabed.

definition.text: The depth bands of the deep ocean: the bathyal, abyssal and hadal zones.

facts.text: The bathyal zone, or continental slope, runs from 200 to 3,000 meters and mixes elements of the shelf and the abyss.
The abyssal zone lies between 3–6 km deep, and the hadal zone between 6–11 km.

definition.text: Deep-sea communities around hydrothermal vents that are powered by chemosynthetic bacteria rather than sunlight.

facts.text: They are among the few ecosystems on the planet that do not depend on sunlight for energy.
Tube worms such as Riftia live in partnership with chemosynthetic bacteria.
Water leaving 'black smoker' chimneys can reach 400 °C (752 °F), kept from boiling by high pressure.
